newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish "love doctor" offers cure for lonely hearts.
newsitem.headline: Irish "love doctor" offers cure for lonely hearts.

text.p: Lonely? The love doctor of Lisdoonvarna would like to hear from you.
If you're looking for a husband or wife, head for the little town in the west of Ireland where an annual matchmaking festival attracts 25,000 lonely hearts each year.
Nestling in the heart of the scenic Burren region in north County Clare, the village is the focus of the festival which draws people from all over the world.
Local farmer Willie Daly is Lisdoonvarna's most famous citizen because of his skill in finding suitable partners for thousands of lonely hearts.
Locals call the white-bearded and ruddy-faced farmer "the love doctor".
"In the last few weeks I've made about 400 introductions but I don't know how many marriages will result," Daly told Reuters over hot whiskey in Twoomey's Tavern on a wet Lisdoonvarna day.
"Most women look for farmers, big farmers," he said. "There seems to be a new interest in farmers and lots of professional women are looking for them. Farming seems to be a trendy thing again."
Daly said women have become more discriminating in their choice of men in recent years.

"With women's equality and all that, women are looking more for love and romance rather than a roof over their heads or a few acres of land like long ago. Women are a bit more choosy and sophisticated nowadays," he said.
As for men, Daly says they look for "teachers or nurses -- but only healthy and honest ones".
Daly has a famous red matchmaking book which contains the personal details of thousands of people looking for suitable partners for friendship or marriage.
The book has been in his family for three generations and dates back to the turn of the century when his grandfather arranged matches.
A few years ago the red book went missing but was eventually found in a peat bog by Daly's children.
"It was all wet and soggy, but we dried it out and it was good as new. Over one hundred years of matchmaking history would have been lost," he said.

Everyone in Lisdoonvarna knows Daly. On the narrow, cobbled streets of the town people shout greetings or stop to discuss marriage or the weather, and in the small pubs and dance halls, where people gather to drink Guinness and waltz to traditional Irish music, his services are much in demand.
"Autumn is a busy time for matchmaking with the long lonely nights," he said, finishing his whiskey and setting off for another Lisdoonvarna pub, the cosy Matchmakers Bar.

As he arrives, a group of people gather round and Daly begins making matches. After a brief introduction, he pairs off Meg, a reserved Dublin woman, with a straw-hatted West Clare farmer called Johnjoe.
Both go for a dance with disastrous results. Meg storms back to Daly leaving Johnjoe stranded mid-waltz. "He can't dance," she shrieks. "He must have a wooden leg or something."
In another corner of the bar, Lucy Reeves, an office worker from Florida, was deep in conversation with three men. She told Reuters it was her third time at the Lisdoonvarna festival.
"I keep coming back for the Guinness and the scenery and the wonderful handsome Irishmen," she said, winking at her three companions.

Daly says he also runs "Love Trail" pony treks for couples who want more time together. The treks through the wild, unspoilt countryside of County Clare last for six days and Daly says couples who take part become very close and romance often blossoms.
Daly has been matchmaking for 30 years. His service was free until recently but he has now begun charging male clients.

Women are still matched up free of charge, however. Daly says there is a shortage of marriagable women in the west of Ireland and he wants to attract more eligible females to register in his famous red book.
